rows.description: A teenager who drags out a word such as fiiine may signal reluctance, boredom or sarcasm. The rhythm can contradict the words, so a friend or parent reads both, then asks a gentle check.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager whose speech races when anxious can practise measured pace by pausing at full stops and breathing out first. A steadier pace often helps the speaker feel calmer as well as sound calmer.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anxiety, calm, relief from stress

rows.description: A teenager who waits hours for a message reply may be busy, unsure what to say or upset. Reading a delay as rejection is a common pitfall, so asking directly is wiser than spiralling.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager who falls silent or stops abruptly mid-sentence may be hurt, embarrassed, angry or simply thinking. Silence is ambiguous, so a caring reply gives space and leaves the door open to talk later.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anger, embarrassment, hurt

rows.description: A teenager sings along with favourite songs or croons privately to express longing, pride or belonging to a group. Lyrics chosen may mirror mood, but they are not proof of what the teen feels.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager may hum or sing under headphones to calm nerves before an exam or after conflict. Singing can lower tension, and it is a healthy tool alongside talking with a trusted person.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager may use slang, nicknames, emojis or a nod as a greeting; changes in greeting style from a friend may signal closeness or distance. Reading too much into one missed reply is a common pitfall.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager uses examples, analogies and diagrams to illustrate a point and persuade peers. Vivid examples help, though they can also be cherry-picked, so checking sources matters.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager who reports something to an adult may be seeking safety or seeking revenge. Adults thank the teen, listen without assuming motives and act on safety concerns.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager asks for confirmation such as so you are saying and probes for reasons. Probing can feel supportive or like interrogation, depending on tone and relationship.
